clue.text: Badge from Britain GI sniper brought back

indicators.note: 'from' says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows
something brought back returns the way it came, so the run is read right to left

blocks.note: the letters sit across these three words, ready to be read backwards

explanation.surface: A soldier's badge taken from a British-based American sniper.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'BritAIN GI SNIper' backwards to find INSIGNIA; GI is an American soldier, which suits the badge picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Insignia are the emblems or badges of rank or membership, so the plural noun serves for a badge.

clue.text: What does foot have three times as many of as hand?

definitions.text: What does foot have three times as many of as hand?

blocks.note: surface reading: a body part at the end of the leg; setter's reading: a unit of length, twelve of a smaller unit
surface reading: the body part; setter's reading: the unit used to measure horses, a third of a foot

explanation.walkthrough: The question sounds like anatomy, toes against fingers, but foot and hand are both units of length: a foot is twelve of the answer and a hand four.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the small imperial unit of length, twelve to a foot and four to a hand.

clue.text: Stamina required to cross river or brook

indicators.note: to cross something here is to straddle it, so one word spans the other and holds it inside

blocks.note: steam is energy or stamina, as in running out of steam
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: It takes stamina to get across a river or a brook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' is just a link here; the river R sits inside STEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: A stream is a small natural watercourse, the same thing as a brook.

clue.text: Where this isn't from and the kind of animal it isn't

definitions.text: Where this isn't from and the kind of animal it isn't

blocks.note: the first word of the answer is a West African country, yet the animal comes from South America

blocks.clueFragment: the kind of animal it isn't
blocks.note: the second word names a farm animal, yet the creature is a rodent

explanation.walkthrough: The riddle describes a pet named after a place it does not come from and an animal it is not.
explanation.definitionFit: The guinea pig is a South American rodent, the cavy, neither from Guinea nor a pig.

clue.text: Popular work in art gallery in recycled clay? Not exactly

indicators.note: something recycled is broken down and reused in a new form, so these letters are rearranged
'in' places the gallery work inside the reworked letters

blocks.note: in means fashionable or popular
the letters to be rearranged
to curate is to organise an exhibition, the work done in a gallery

explanation.surface: A popular gallery installation made from recycled clay, described only roughly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' appears twice with two jobs: first it is a word meaning popular, then it is the signal for putting one piece inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: Inaccurately means not precisely or not correctly, so it matches the adverb phrase not exactly.

clue.text: Argument as result of being oddly selective in formal clause

indicators.text: as result of being oddly selective in
indicators.note: being oddly selective means keeping only the first, third, fifth and further odd-placed letters

blocks.note: the odd-placed letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A dispute arising because someone picked and chose oddly in the wording of a formal clause.
explanation.definitionFit: A fracas is a noisy quarrel or brawl, so it is a heated argument.

clue.text: November is equally far away for him and his beloved

blocks.note: in the NATO phonetic alphabet November stands for N, four letters from R and four from J
the lover and his beloved are the code words for R and J, the Shakespearean pair

explanation.walkthrough: November sounds like a month, but it is a word in the radio alphabet; the code words for J and R are the names of Shakespeare's star-crossed lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's young lover, whose beloved is Juliet, shares his name with the NATO code word for R.

clue.text: Service provider for other service providers?

definitions.text: Service provider for other service providers?

blocks.note: surface reading: a business that supplies a service; setter's reading: a cleric who leads religious services
surface reading: rival companies; setter's reading: members of the armed services

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase sounds like business jargon, but a religious service is meant, held for people serving in the forces.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplain is a clergyman attached to an institution such as a regiment or ship, holding services for military personnel.

clue.text: Piercing, small missile

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
Trident is a submarine-launched nuclear missile

explanation.surface: A small missile that pierces its target.
explanation.walkthrough: Piercing looks like a description of what a missile does, but it is the definition, meaning shrill.
explanation.definitionFit: A strident sound is loud and harsh, so piercing in the sense of an ear-splitting noise.

clue.text: Sex returns in erotic festival

indicators.note: something that returns goes back the way it came, so the letters are read in the opposite order
'in' puts the reversed piece inside the word for erotic

blocks.note: carnal means sexual, fleshly
sex is Latin for six, the Roman numeral VI

explanation.surface: Sex makes a comeback at a racy festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sex' is not about passion at all: it is the Latin word for six, so a Roman numeral is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A carnival is a public festival with processions and merrymaking, often before Lent.

clue.text: One's piano tune better? Just the opposite

blocks.note: one is I, and I's means I am, giving I'M
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
an air is a tune or melody

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether retuning their piano improves it, and is told it makes it worse.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole phrase 'better? Just the opposite': the opposite of to better is to make worse.
explanation.definitionFit: To impair is to weaken or damage, the reverse of improving something, so it is the antonym of the verb better.

clue.text: Right work among collected writings for man's study?

indicators.note: something among a collection sits inside it, so these letters go within the word for collected writings

blocks.note: an anthology is a collection of writings
R is the abbreviation for right
OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: The proper work to include in an anthology about humankind.
explanation.walkthrough: OP, short for opus, is the standard crossword stand-in for a work; 'man' here means humankind in general.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthropology is the scientific study of humankind, man in the old general sense, its societies and cultures.

clue.text: Times editor's leader subject to deletion

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so only the first letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: an era is a period of time, times
the apostrophe-s taken as written
the first letter of editor

explanation.surface: The newspaper's chief editor faces having their work cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper but just means eras, and 'editor's' is split so the S joins ERA before the E.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase is to subject something to deletion, rubbing or wiping it out; the phrase works as a verb.

clue.text: Silly person in rogue's embrace carried on amorously

indicators.note: 'in' says the silly person goes inside the other word
an embrace wraps arms around someone, so the rogue's word surrounds the other

blocks.note: a cad is a rogue or bounder
a noodle is a fool, a silly person

explanation.surface: A fool in a scoundrel's arms behaved amorously.
explanation.walkthrough: The embrace suits the amorous surface, but here it only means one word wraps round the other; noodle is informal for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: To canoodle is to kiss and cuddle, so canoodled means behaved amorously, a past tense matching carried on.

clue.text: Running in fear

blocks.note: first meaning: arrest, as when police run a suspect in
second meaning: anxiety or dread about what may happen

explanation.walkthrough: The three words read as someone fleeing in terror, but split after 'in': running someone in is slang for arresting them.
explanation.definitionFit: Apprehension means both the arrest of a suspect and uneasy anxiety about the future.

clue.text: In short, disoriented sailor following new navigational aid

indicators.note: something disoriented has lost its bearings, so the letters end up out of order
'following' puts the sailor and the jumbled letters after the letter for new

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
the letters to be rearranged
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A lost sailor, put briefly, relies on a fresh way of finding direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' reads as 'briefly', but 'short' is the fodder; a disoriented sailor would indeed want this star.
explanation.definitionFit: The North Star, Polaris, stays almost fixed over the North Pole, so sailors have long steered by it.

clue.text: Oddly cued a Conservative cut, as one not liking to see class struggle?

definitions.text: one not liking to see class struggle?

indicators.note: done oddly means done in a strange way, so these letters are rearranged
something cut is shortened, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A Tory who wants to stop class struggle, the opposite of a Marxist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'class struggle' looks political, but it means pupils struggling in a classroom, which a teacher hates to see.
explanation.definitionFit: An educator is a teacher, someone who wants pupils in a class to do well rather than struggle.

clue.text: Minimal idea following article in examination

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
the indefinite article
taken as written
a test is an examination

explanation.surface: Having the faintest idea after reading an article in an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minimal idea' suggests the definition is the phrase 'faintest idea'; the definition is just 'Minimal', with 'idea' completing the familiar phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Faintest means slightest or least, the smallest possible amount, as in not the faintest notion.

clue.text: Level playing area for would-be kingmakers

definitions.text: Level playing area for would-be kingmakers

blocks.note: surface reading: a flat sports pitch, with a nod to a level playing field
setter's reading: pieces in a board game that hope to reach the far side and be crowned kings

explanation.walkthrough: Kingmakers suggests political power-brokers, but in draughts (checkers) a piece reaching the back row is crowned a king, and the game is played on a flat board.
explanation.definitionFit: The board for draughts, the British name for checkers, is flat and is where players try to promote pieces to kings.

clue.text: Lose track of mass whisky producer

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for mass
Islay is a Scottish island famous for its malt whiskies

explanation.surface: A distillery loses track of a large quantity of its whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: Islay is an island of the Inner Hebrides off Scotland's west coast, home to many distilleries.
explanation.definitionFit: To mislay something is to put it down and forget where, so to lose track of it.

clue.text: Ending article uploaded into document

indicators.note: in a down clue, loaded upwards means the letters are read from the bottom up
'into' places the turned word inside the word for document

blocks.note: a file is a document
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: The final article is uploaded to a document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uploaded' sounds like computing, but in a down light it means the word is written upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A finale is the closing part of a show or piece of music, its ending.

clue.text: Singer making mess of carol, not keeping time

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it inside, so the time letter goes within the other letters
making a mess of something jumbles it up, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A singer botches a carol by failing to stay in time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not keeping time' reads as bad rhythm, but NOT is fodder and 'keeping time' adds a T.
explanation.definitionFit: A contralto is a female singer with the lowest female voice range.

clue.text: You need to be careful when one charges you money

definitions.text: You need to be careful when one charges you

blocks.clueFragment: You need to be careful when one charges you
blocks.note: first meaning: a large horned animal known for charging
second meaning: an old British slang word for cash

explanation.walkthrough: 'charges you money' reads as a bill, but split before 'money': the charging is a stampeding beast.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhinoceros is notorious for charging, and rhino is dated British slang for cash.

clue.text: Panama, perhaps, annexing island with one Caribbean state

indicators.note: a territory that annexes another takes it within its borders, so one letter goes inside

blocks.note: a Panama is a kind of straw hat
I is the abbreviation for island
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Panama the country seizing an island to form a Caribbean state.
explanation.walkthrough: Panama looks like the nation next door, but a Panama is a straw hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Haiti is an independent country occupying the western part of the Caribbean island of Hispaniola.

clue.text: Article is about singular line of argument

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so the preceding words wrap around the letter for singular

blocks.note: the definite article
taken as written
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: A newspaper article concerns a single argument.
explanation.walkthrough: THE and IS together surround S: THE(S)IS.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesis is a proposition advanced and argued for, the central line of argument in a piece of writing.

clue.text: Cultivate area on right side of hill to provide food in Mexico

indicators.note: being on the right side of something means coming after it when read left to right

blocks.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor
to till is to cultivate the soil
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A farmer plants the sunny side of a hill to grow food in Mexico.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky outcrop on a hill, a common word in the English West Country; the tilled area goes to its right.
explanation.definitionFit: A tortilla is a thin flatbread of maize or wheat, a staple Mexican food.

clue.text: Restrict food from ten to nine, say, finishing at noon

indicators.note: a word's finish is its last letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: ten to nine, 10:9, is an example of a ratio
the last letter of noon

explanation.surface: Meals are restricted to a window from about ten to nine until midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ten to nine' looks like a time of day, 8:50, but is a proportion, 10 to 9.
explanation.definitionFit: To ration is to limit the amount of food or supplies each person may have.

clue.text: For example, that's what's seen in some poetry

definitions.text: For example, that's what's seen in some poetry

blocks.note: setter's reading: 'that' and 'what' look as if they should rhyme on the page but are not pronounced alike
surface reading: a vague description of something found in verse, with 'seen' hinting the rhyme exists only for the eye

explanation.walkthrough: The clue's own words 'that' and 'what' are the example: they look alike in spelling but sound different, a pairing that works only on sight.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye rhyme is a pair of words spelled as if they rhyme but pronounced differently, like love and move.
